clinicalPearls: Progressive, usually cephalocaudal loss of subcutaneous fat beginning in the face and upper body, often sparing or accumulating fat over the hips and legs
Typically starts in childhood or adolescence, more often in females, and may follow a febrile illness
Strongly linked to low serum complement C3 and the presence of C3 nephritic factor, which stabilises the alternative-pathway convertase
Membranoproliferative (mesangiocapillary) glomerulonephritis, classically type II/dense-deposit disease, is an important associated renal complication
Unlike the generalised forms, severe insulin resistance, diabetes, and hypertriglyceridaemia are comparatively uncommon because lower-body fat is preserved
Leptin is often relatively preserved, so leptin (metreleptin) replacement has a limited role compared with generalised lipodystrophy
Management focuses on monitoring for and treating the associated renal disease and any autoimmune features rather than on metabolic reversal
Diagnosis rests on the characteristic upper-body fat-loss pattern, complement studies (C3, C3 nephritic factor), and renal assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Acquired partial lipodystrophy is a progressive loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue that characteristically begins in the face and spreads downward over the trunk and arms while sparing or expanding fat in the lower body. It is closely associated with dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway: many patients have low C3 and circulating C3 nephritic factor, an autoantibody that stabilises the C3 convertase and promotes complement-mediated adipocyte lysis, particularly in fat expressing high levels of complement factor D (adipsin). The same complement dysregulation underlies the linked membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Because lower-body fat depots persist, the severe insulin resistance typical of generalised lipodystrophy is usually absent.
additionalDifferentials: Cushing syndrome (facial and truncal fat changes)
Localised lipoatrophy from injections or panniculitis
Ageing-related or constitutional facial fat loss
Dermatomyositis or other connective-tissue disease with fat changes
additionalInvestigations: Serum complement C3 (often low) and assay for C3 nephritic factor
Renal function, urinalysis, and urine protein to detect glomerulonephritis
Renal biopsy where membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is suspected
Regional fat imaging (DEXA/MRI) to map the upper-body fat-loss pattern
Metabolic panel (glucose, lipids, insulin) which is often near-normal
Autoimmune and connective-tissue screen where clinically indicated
redFlags: Proteinuria, haematuria, or declining renal function signalling glomerulonephritis
Features of associated systemic autoimmune disease
Progressive disfiguring fat loss with psychological impact
reference.prognosis: The metabolic outlook is generally more favourable than in generalised lipodystrophy because lower-body fat is retained, but long-term prognosis is dominated by the risk of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, which can progress to chronic kidney disease.
pitfalls: Assuming the severe insulin resistance of generalised forms and over-investigating for it
Failing to check complement and screen for associated renal disease
Mistaking the facial fat loss for ageing or an eating disorder
Offering leptin replacement despite often near-normal leptin levels
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on lipodystrophy
management: Nephrology-led management of associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, including renin-angiotensin blockade for proteinuria and immunosuppression where indicated
Periodic surveillance of renal function, urinalysis and complement (C3 and C3 nephritic factor) for onset or progression of glomerulonephritis
Reconstructive options for facial lipoatrophy such as autologous fat transfer or dermal fillers, as metreleptin has limited value given relatively preserved leptin
Monitor for the usually mild metabolic disturbance in glucose and lipids rather than the severe insulin resistance of the generalised forms
Screen for coexisting autoimmune and connective-tissue disease
Multidisciplinary care spanning endocrinology, nephrology and plastic surgery
